newsitem.title: USA: Environmentalists to fight Lafarge plan.
newsitem.headline: Environmentalists to fight Lafarge plan.

text.p: Environmentalists said they were gearing up Thursday to fight Lafarge Corp's proposal to dig a limestone quarry in a section of the Everglades that the U.S. Congress has decided to buy as part of an effort to save the unique Florida ecosystem.

Lafarge, based in Reston, Va., has filed a permit seeking to dig an 80-foot-deep quarry in 1,131 acres of sawgrass prairie it owns near barriers that separate the Everglades from populated areas south of Miami.
The news angered environmentalists, who maintain that interruptions in the narrow sheet of water that flows through the Everglades could upset the area's ecological balance.

"I think it's a bad idea," said Joe Garcia, spokesman for the Save Our Everglades foundation. "A big old hole like that is just going to be another impedient to the restoration of the proper hydrology."
Environmentalists also speculated Lafarge might have filed the permit to increase the value of the property and thus increase any government offer.
Congress voted last year to buy more than 100,000 acres of Everglades land, part of an effort to restore an ecosystem damaged by chemical runoff from farming and unchecked development.

Ed Junia, vice president for environmental affairs at Lafarge's cement operations in Michigan, said no one from the U.S. government had contacted the company about buying the property, which it has owned since the 1950s. He said revenue from use as a limestone mine would be exponentially higher than the $500 per acre that has been reported as the government's offering price for Everglades property.
He also disputed the contention that the quarry would harm Everglades water flow.

"I think I would respond to that by saying I don't know if that's entirely, entirely true," he said. "The water level in that land is so close to the surface, that by excavating the rock, you are not substantially changing the water flows or water supplies. The areas that we are talking about should not have any significant impact."
